Pregnancy

Isotretinoin and pregnancy: exposure, prevention and acne-care choices

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Oral isotretinoin, sold under names including Roaccutane, can be an effective treatment for severe acne. It can also cause serious harm to a developing pregnancy, so it must not be used during pregnancy. If you are pregnant, think you may be pregnant or have a positive pregnancy test while taking it, stop taking isotretinoin and contact your prescriber and maternity or pregnancy-care team immediately. Exposure needs prompt specialist assessment; it does not by itself tell you what will happen to an individual pregnancy.

Know which medicine you are taking

Isotretinoin is a retinoid related to vitamin A. Oral capsules are used for severe acne when appropriate other treatment has not worked. Roaccutane is one brand; names, formulations and availability differ between countries. Accutane is a familiar historical brand name. Check the active ingredient and exact product rather than relying on the name someone remembers.

Dose, food instructions and treatment length are individualized. A course usually lasts months, but there is no single duration that applies to everyone, and different formulations are not automatically interchangeable. Oral isotretinoin is also different from other oral retinoids and from creams containing retinoids. Do not apply one medicine’s pregnancy waiting period or exposure-risk estimate to another.

Act immediately if pregnancy is possible

If you become pregnant, suspect pregnancy or have a positive test while taking isotretinoin, stop the capsules and contact your prescriber immediately. Also contact your maternity or pregnancy-care team so that specialist advice can be arranged. Tell them the exact product, dose, dates taken, last dose, pregnancy-test results and estimated pregnancy dates. Do not wait for a routine acne appointment or for symptoms to appear.

If contraception failed or you had sex that could cause pregnancy during the prevention interval, get same-day advice from your prescriber and a sexual-health service or pharmacist. If you are still taking isotretinoin, stop it while obtaining that advice. Emergency contraception is time-sensitive, so do not wait for a missed period or a later pregnancy test before asking about it. An early negative test does not exclude a very recent pregnancy; follow the team’s testing and restart instructions rather than restarting yourself.

Understand the risk without treating a percentage as a prediction

Isotretinoin is a known human teratogen: exposure during pregnancy can cause birth defects and increases the risk of pregnancy loss. Even a small amount or a short exposure can matter. There is no established safe dose or safe period for using oral isotretinoin during pregnancy. Treatment should not continue simply because a scan has not yet shown a problem.

Published estimates vary with the pregnancies studied, exposure timing, outcome measured and follow-up. Miscarriage, structural birth defects and later developmental difficulties are different outcomes with different denominators. A single percentage cannot predict an individual pregnancy, and exposure does not mean that every pregnancy will be affected. Specialist counselling should explain the available evidence, its uncertainty and the options relevant to you without blame or pressure.

What fetal effects are described, and what tests can show

Reported isotretinoin embryopathy includes abnormalities of the ears and face, cleft palate, eyes, skull or brain, heart and central nervous system. Abnormal development of the thymus or parathyroid glands is also described. Learning or behavioural difficulties can occur, including in children without an obvious structural abnormality at birth. An increased chance of premature birth and low birth weight has also been reported; these outcomes need individual assessment too.

After exposure, the team may arrange a specialist review and ultrasound assessment appropriate to the pregnancy and local service. Ultrasound can look for some structural problems and assess growth, but a normal scan cannot rule out every effect. There is no prenatal test that can predict all later learning or behavioural outcomes. Discuss what each proposed test can and cannot answer, rather than treating either a normal test or an exposure history as a complete prognosis.

Plan the interval before trying to conceive

Current isotretinoin guidance generally requires avoiding pregnancy for at least one month before starting, throughout treatment and for at least one month after the last dose. Follow the exact product and local pregnancy-prevention instructions, including the required post-treatment test and confirmation of when you can try to conceive. Finishing the capsules does not mean the prevention plan ends that day.

A routine three-month wait is not the standard interval in the current isotretinoin guidance checked here. If a clinician recommends a different interval, ask whether it relates to your exact medicine or circumstances. Other retinoids can have very different restrictions. Do not shorten an interval yourself, but do not assume that a rule for another retinoid applies to isotretinoin either.

Use a written contraception and testing plan

Before treatment, discuss whether you could become pregnant and which prevention methods meet your programme’s requirements. In the United States, the iPLEDGE REMS has specific contraception or qualifying abstinence requirements for patients who can become pregnant. UK requirements are framed differently, including a highly effective method or appropriate complementary methods. Your own medical history, other medicines and ability to use a method consistently matter.

Pregnancy tests are required before treatment and during and after the course according to the applicable programme, commonly with monthly monitoring for those who can become pregnant. A test is not a substitute for contraception. Ask where tests must be performed, who reviews the result, what to do after a missed test or contraceptive problem, and when prescriptions can be issued. Do not declare yourself exempt or rely on a partner’s vasectomy as a reason to bypass the programme’s assessment.

iPLEDGE is a United States programme, not a worldwide rule

The US iPLEDGE Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy applies to FDA-approved isotretinoin products. Patients, prescribers and dispensing pharmacies have enrolment and participation responsibilities. Patient requirements depend on the reproductive-risk category, so pregnancy-testing and contraception duties differ between categories. Being sexually inactive does not by itself remove the need to follow enrolment and category-specific instructions.

US testing and administrative requirements are changing. As of this article’s review on 6 November 2026, the FDA had scheduled implementation of further changes for 15 November 2026, alongside existing enforcement-discretion arrangements. Do not treat an announced future change as permission to alter testing now. Ask your registered prescriber or pharmacy for the current instructions for your next test and prescription; a general article cannot replace the programme’s individual requirements.

Outside the US, follow the local prevention programme

The UK Pregnancy Prevention Programme requires assessment, information, contraception and pregnancy testing for patients who could become pregnant. Current product guidance describes prevention beginning at least one month before treatment, continuing during it and for one month afterwards. The prescriber should make sure that you understand the risk and the plan. A US website registration is not a substitute for the programme in your country.

Other prescribing safeguards can also change. The MHRA’s January 2026 update removed the UK requirement for a second prescriber’s agreement for patients under 18, while retaining pregnancy-prevention and mental-health and sexual-function safeguards. Discuss your own circumstances privately with the clinical team. Do not use an old leaflet, another country’s exemption or another person’s prescription as your treatment plan.

Do not donate blood or share capsules

Do not donate blood while taking isotretinoin or for one month after the last dose. This restriction helps prevent a pregnant recipient from receiving blood containing the medicine, and it is not limited to patients who can become pregnant themselves. Tell the blood-donation service about treatment and follow its eligibility instructions.

Never share isotretinoin, even with someone whose acne looks similar. Return unused capsules as advised by your pharmacist and keep them away from children and anyone for whom they were not prescribed. Do not use vitamin A supplements or another acne medicine alongside isotretinoin without checking; some combinations, including tetracycline antibiotics, can be harmful.

Balance acne treatment, conception plans and breastfeeding

If you are planning pregnancy, discuss the timing before starting a course. You may choose a different acne treatment or complete an appropriate course and the required prevention and follow-up interval before trying to conceive. Discuss the impact of acne and your priorities so the plan fits your health and pregnancy intentions. Make a plan with your dermatologist and pregnancy-care clinician.

After birth, do not restart isotretinoin automatically if you are breastfeeding. It is not recommended during breastfeeding, and product guidance may specify a further interval after the last dose before feeding can resume. That interval is a separate question from the one-month pregnancy-prevention period. Ask about the exact product and a suitable feeding and acne-treatment plan; do not use another brand’s interval as personal clearance.

A father’s treatment is a different exposure question

Treatment in a male partner does not expose a pregnancy in the same way as the pregnant person taking oral isotretinoin. UK product information indicates that the amount in semen is too low to be expected to cause the medicine’s fetal effects. Available paternal evidence has limits; reports about sexual function or sperm changes do not establish that a partner’s treatment causes birth defects.

If you have fertility concerns, sexual symptoms or questions about trying to conceive while a partner takes isotretinoin, discuss them with the prescriber rather than applying maternal restrictions to both partners automatically. The patient must still follow their own local programme, must not share capsules and must observe the blood-donation restriction. A partner’s treatment never makes it safe for a pregnant person to take the medicine.

Choose pregnancy-compatible acne treatment by ingredient

Pregnancy-related hormonal changes can worsen acne, but oral isotretinoin is not a treatment option during pregnancy. A dermatologist or pregnancy-care clinician can consider alternatives according to severity and the exact ingredient. Options may include azelaic acid, limited use of benzoyl peroxide or selected prescription treatments. Do not assume that every oral antibiotic, cream or over-the-counter acne product is suitable.

Topical retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy too, although their absorption and exposure evidence differ from oral isotretinoin. Review products containing retinol or retinoids and any supplements with the team. During breastfeeding, a topical product also needs assessment for direct contact with the baby, particularly on the breast or nipple. Do not transfer a reassurance about one ingredient to an unlabelled mixture or an entire product category.

Keep daily care gentle and realistic

Use a gentle cleanser up to twice daily and after sweating, rather than scrubbing or washing repeatedly. Remove make-up before bed and choose non-comedogenic, non-greasy skin-care and cosmetic products when possible. Make-up is optional; acne does not mean that you have failed to keep clean. Avoid picking spots and repeatedly changing several products at once.

A balanced diet, ordinary hydration and clean items that touch your face can support everyday comfort, but they do not replace effective acne treatment or prevent isotretinoin-related pregnancy harm. A fixed weekly pillowcase schedule, avoiding all make-up or drinking extra water is not a proven cure. Check sunscreen and other skin products with your clinician if they irritate your skin or you are unsure about an ingredient.

Know which follow-up needs immediate help

Pregnancy, suspected pregnancy or a positive test during isotretinoin treatment needs immediate stopping and contact with the prescriber and pregnancy-care team. Possible contraceptive failure needs same-day advice, including time-sensitive emergency-contraception assessment when relevant. Keep a record of the medicine and dates, but do not delay contact to assemble a perfect history. Do not restart after an exposure concern without the prescriber’s instructions.

If you have taken more than prescribed, obtain urgent medical advice immediately, even if you feel well. Suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment; while awaiting help, do not induce vomiting or give anything to eat or drink. Breathing difficulty, swelling of the tongue or throat, fainting or loss of consciousness can indicate a medical emergency: call local emergency services. Serious self-injury or inability to keep yourself or someone else safe also needs emergency help. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance. If depression, a mood disturbance, hallucinations or other symptoms of psychosis, or aggressive behaviour develops, stop isotretinoin and contact the prescriber immediately; stopping alone may not be enough, and further assessment may be needed. New or worsening sexual-function or other concerning symptoms need prompt discussion with the prescriber rather than waiting until the end of the course.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Write down the exact product, dose, treatment dates, pregnancy tests and contraception plan. Contact the prescriber immediately about pregnancy and the same day about a possible contraceptive failure; do not wait to complete the record.

Before trying to conceive, donating blood or restarting after birth, confirm the relevant waiting, testing and feeding instructions for your product and country. Do not substitute another medicine’s or programme’s rules.

Bring all acne medicines, cosmetics and supplements to an ingredient review, agree suitable alternatives and ask what an exposure assessment or scan can and cannot establish.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare a private medication timeline, appointment reminders and questions for the prescribing or pregnancy-care team. It cannot determine whether exposure harmed a pregnancy, interpret a test as an all-clear, choose contraception, replace a prevention-programme record or authorize treatment to restart. Do not delay urgent contact while entering information.

When to seek help

If pregnant, possibly pregnant or testing positive during isotretinoin treatment, stop the capsules and contact the prescriber and pregnancy-care team immediately. If contraception failed, stop ongoing treatment and seek same-day advice about pregnancy risk, emergency contraception when relevant, testing and restarting. Taking more than prescribed needs immediate medical advice; suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment. While waiting for poisoning help, do not induce vomiting or give food or drink. Breathing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness, serious self-injury or inability to keep anyone safe needs local emergency services. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Do not share capsules or donate blood during treatment or for one month afterwards.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • If pregnant or possibly pregnant while taking isotretinoin, stop the capsules and contact the prescriber and pregnancy-care team immediately.
  • Exposure can cause serious harm, but neither a percentage nor a normal scan can predict every individual outcome.
  • Follow the exact medicine’s prevention, testing and waiting plan; US iPLEDGE and UK rules are not interchangeable.
  • Do not donate blood during treatment or for one month afterwards, and never share capsules.
  • Plan pregnancy and breastfeeding before starting or restarting treatment, and choose acne alternatives by ingredient with a clinician.

Frequently asked questions

What is Roaccutane?

Roaccutane is a brand of oral isotretinoin, a retinoid used for severe acne. Brand names and formulations vary, and treatment is individualized. It must not be taken during pregnancy. Check the active ingredient and product instructions rather than assuming that another retinoid or a topical cream has the same rules.

What are the risks if isotretinoin is taken during pregnancy?

It increases the risk of pregnancy loss and can cause serious structural birth defects and developmental difficulties. Even short exposure can matter, but not every exposed pregnancy has the same outcome. Published percentages cannot provide an individual prediction, and prenatal tests cannot rule out all later learning effects. Stop the medicine and contact the prescriber and pregnancy-care team immediately for specialist assessment.

How long should I wait after isotretinoin before trying to conceive?

Current isotretinoin guidance generally requires avoiding pregnancy for at least one month after the final dose, as well as before and throughout treatment. Complete the required post-treatment testing and confirm the timing with your prescriber. A routine three-month wait is not the standard in the guidance checked here; other retinoids or individual circumstances may require different advice.

Which birth defects are associated with exposure?

Reported effects include abnormalities of the ears, face or palate, eyes, skull or brain, heart, central nervous system, thymus and parathyroid glands. Learning or behavioural effects may occur without an obvious birth defect. This is a description of reported effects, not a prediction that a particular baby will have them. Specialist counselling and appropriate scans can clarify some questions but cannot guarantee the future outcome.

What should I do if contraception fails during treatment?

If you are still taking isotretinoin, stop it and obtain same-day advice from your prescriber and a sexual-health service or pharmacist. Emergency contraception is time-sensitive, so do not wait for a missed period or a later pregnancy test before asking. Follow the team’s testing and restart instructions; an early negative test does not exclude a very recent pregnancy. A positive test or suspected pregnancy needs immediate prescriber and pregnancy-care contact.

Does everyone need the same iPLEDGE tests and contraception?

No. iPLEDGE is a US programme with enrolment requirements and duties based on reproductive-risk category. It is not a worldwide programme, and UK or other local rules differ. Follow current instructions from your registered prescriber and pharmacy, including where tests must be performed. Announced future changes are not permission to change today’s plan yourself.

Can I restart after birth, breastfeed, or rely on my partner’s treatment being safe?

Do not restart isotretinoin during breastfeeding without a specialist plan; it is not recommended, and any post-treatment feeding interval depends on the product. This is separate from the conception waiting period. A male partner’s treatment is not expected to expose a pregnancy like maternal oral treatment, but fertility or sexual concerns merit review. Neither situation permits sharing capsules or bypassing local prescribing requirements.

What acne care and urgent help should I use instead?

Ask a clinician about ingredient-specific alternatives such as azelaic acid or limited benzoyl peroxide rather than choosing any OTC product or antibiotic. Keep cleansing gentle and avoid unproven diet or hygiene cures. Pregnancy or suspected pregnancy on isotretinoin needs immediate stopping and prescriber contact; a contraceptive failure needs same-day advice. Taking more than prescribed needs immediate medical advice; suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment without inducing vomiting or giving food or drink while waiting. Breathing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness, serious self-injury or inability to keep anyone safe requires emergency help. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
